result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.plot_cosmo()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Display the graph as an interactive Cosmograph widget in a Jupyter notebook. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.plot_cosmo()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Display the graph as an interactive Cosmograph widget in a Jupyter notebook. title: >- [Graph.plot_cosmo()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Display the graph as an interactive Cosmograph widget in a Jupyter notebook. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Display the graph as an interactive Cosmograph widget in a Jupyter notebook. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L4377-L4486){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.plot_cosmo( point_color_by=None, point_size_by=None, link_color_by=None, link_width_by=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Requires the `cosmograph` package (`pip install cosmograph`). The widget uses GPU-accelerated WebGL rendering and handles millions of nodes/edges in the browser. Unlike `plot_vis()`, Cosmograph renders only as a Jupyter widget and there is no browser fallback. Call this method in a notebook cell and evaluate the returned widget to display it. The node and edge DataFrames (as returned by `get_node_df()` and `get_edge_df()`) are handed to Cosmograph as its points and links tables. Nodes are identified by their `id` column, edges by their `source` and `target` columns, and nodes are labelled with their `label` column. All other columns are included in the widget, so they can be inspected interactively. Layout is computed in the browser by Cosmograph's own force simulation. Reach for `plot_cosmo()` when a graph is too large for `plot()` or `plot_vis()` to stay responsive (tens of thousands of nodes and up), or when you want to explore a large network interactively after computing communities or centralities. The four `*_by` parameters map DataFrame columns to visual channels, so any attribute you've stored on the nodes or edges (including computed ones) can drive the encoding. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [point_color_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of a node DataFrame column to use for point colour encoding, such as `"type"`, a community column created by `cmty_louvain()`, or any custom node attribute. If `None` (default), Cosmograph's default point colour is used. [point_size_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of a node DataFrame column to use for point size encoding. A numeric column such as `"degree"` or a centrality score works best. If `None` (default), all points share Cosmograph's default size. [link_color_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of an edge DataFrame column to use for link colour encoding, such as `"rel"`. If `None` (default), Cosmograph's default link colour is used. [link_width_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of an edge DataFrame column to use for link width encoding, typically a numeric column like `"weight"`. If `None` (default), all links share the default width. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [cosmograph.Cosmograph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : An interactive Cosmograph widget. Evaluate it in a notebook cell to display. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ImportError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the `cosmograph` package is not installed. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~plot_vis`) : A draggable view for small and medium graphs. [](`~plot`) : A static SVG drawing, for reports and web pages. [](`~cmty_louvain`) : Find communities to color the points by. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The node DataFrame's columns are what the `*_by` parameters refer to. Zachary's karate club stores each member's `faction`, and every graph has a `degree` column, so those can drive point colour and size: ::: {#b873ff46 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec club = ec.karate_club() club.get_node_df().columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['id', 'label', 'type', 'faction', 'role', 'degree'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#654f3788 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} widget = club.plot_cosmo(point_color_by="faction", point_size_by="degree") widget ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Compute community and centrality attributes, then chain directly into `plot_cosmo()` to encode them visually (point color reflects community membership, and point size reflects centrality). Cosmograph's WebGL rendering keeps this physics collaboration network of about 12,000 nodes interactive: ::: {#7595320a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} widget = ( ec.physics() .cmty_louvain(attr_name="community") .eigen_centrality(attr_name="centrality") .plot_cosmo( point_color_by="community", point_size_by="centrality", ) ) widget ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: [Interactive widgets](../user-guide/interactive.qmd#large-graphs-with-plot_cosmo) draws the power grid on the GPU, and explains what its four mapping arguments name.
